lessons.title: Red-shift
lessons.summary: Find out how the light from distant galaxies is stretched to longer wavelengths, what this red-shift tells us about an expanding Universe, and how it supports the Big Bang theory while leaving big questions about dark matter and dark energy unanswered.
objectives: I can describe what red-shift is and how it is observed in the light from distant galaxies.
I can explain how red-shift shows that galaxies are moving away from us and that more distant galaxies are moving faster.
I can explain how red-shift provides evidence that the Universe is expanding and supports the Big Bang theory.
I can describe how observations of supernovae suggest the expansion is speeding up and why dark matter and dark energy are still not understood.

activities.title: Stretching light
activities.content:
## What is red-shift?

You have probably noticed how the pitch of an ambulance siren drops as it passes you. Sound waves from a source moving **away** arrive stretched out to a **longer wavelength** and lower frequency. Light behaves in a similar way.

When a light source moves **away** from an observer, the light received has a **longer wavelength** and a **lower frequency** than it had when emitted. Because red is the long-wavelength end of the visible spectrum, the light is said to be **red-shifted**. (A source moving **towards** us gives a **blue-shift**: shorter wavelength, higher frequency.)

### How astronomers see it
Every element absorbs light at its own precise set of wavelengths, producing a pattern of **dark lines** in a star's spectrum, like a barcode. Astronomers know exactly where those lines sit for hydrogen, helium and so on in the laboratory.

In the light from a distant galaxy the **whole barcode is shifted towards the red end**. The pattern is the same, so the same elements are present, but every line has moved to a longer wavelength. The **size of the shift** tells us **how fast** the galaxy is moving away.

The bigger the red-shift, the faster the galaxy is receding.

question.text: Light from a galaxy is observed to be red-shifted. What does this tell us about the galaxy?
question.hint: Red-shift means the wavelength has increased. What kind of motion causes that?
question.explanation: Red-shift means the observed wavelength is longer than expected, which happens when the source is moving away from the observer.

options.text: It is moving away from us

options.feedback: Movement towards us would cause a blue-shift.
Red-shift is about a shift in wavelength, not the colour of the stars.

activities.title: Galaxies are moving apart
activities.content:
## Hubble's discovery

In the 1920s astronomers measured the red-shift of light from many galaxies and found two striking things:

1. The light from **almost every galaxy is red-shifted**. That means nearly all galaxies are **moving away from us**.
2. The **further away** a galaxy is, the **larger its red-shift**, so the **faster it is moving away**. Galaxies twice as far away recede roughly twice as fast.

### What this means
If everything is moving away from us, are we at the centre of the Universe? No. Imagine dots drawn on a balloon that is being blown up. Every dot moves away from every other dot, and dots further apart separate faster, but no dot is the centre. The **space between the galaxies is expanding**.

So the observed red-shifts show that **the whole Universe is expanding**.

### Running the film backwards
If the galaxies are spreading apart now, they must have been **closer together in the past**. Rewind far enough and everything in the Universe would have been packed into a single, extremely small, extremely dense and hot point. This reasoning leads directly to the **Big Bang theory**.

question.text: True or false: galaxies that are further away from Earth show a smaller red-shift than nearby galaxies.
question.hint: Which galaxies are moving away fastest?
question.explanation: False. More distant galaxies are moving away faster and therefore show a larger red-shift.

activities.title: Worked example: comparing galaxies
activities.content:
**Astronomers measure a hydrogen absorption line that is found at 656 nm in the laboratory. In the spectrum of galaxy X it appears at 660 nm; in galaxy Y it appears at 690 nm.**

**Which galaxy is further away?**

Galaxy X: shift = 660 − 656 = 4 nm

Galaxy Y: shift = 690 − 656 = 34 nm

Galaxy Y has the much larger red-shift, so it is moving away much faster. Since speed of recession increases with distance, **galaxy Y is further away**.

**A third galaxy, Z, shows the same line at 654 nm. What does this tell us?**

654 nm is *shorter* than 656 nm: a **blue-shift**. Galaxy Z is moving **towards** us. This does happen for a few very close galaxies (Andromeda is one) whose motion within our local group of galaxies is larger than the expansion of space between them. It does not contradict the expanding Universe; it is a local exception.

**Do we need units?** Red-shift is usually given as a fraction: shift ÷ original wavelength. For galaxy Y that is 34 ÷ 656 = 0.052. Fractions have no units, which is convenient because the same fraction applies to every line in the spectrum.

question.text: A spectral line has a wavelength of 500 nm in the laboratory. In the light from a distant galaxy the same line is observed at 520 nm. Calculate the red-shift as a fraction of the original wavelength. Give your answer as a decimal.
question.hint: Red-shift fraction = (observed wavelength − original wavelength) ÷ original wavelength.

activities.title: The Big Bang theory
activities.content:
## The leading model of the Universe

The **Big Bang theory** says that the Universe began about **13.8 billion years ago** from an extremely **small, hot and dense** region. Space itself then began to expand, and has been expanding ever since, carrying the galaxies apart. The Universe cooled as it expanded, allowing atoms, then stars and galaxies, to form.

### Evidence
1. **Red-shift**: the observed red-shift of galaxies, increasing with distance, shows that the Universe is expanding, exactly as the Big Bang predicts.
2. **Cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR)**: the Big Bang should have released intense radiation that has since been stretched by the expansion to microwave wavelengths. This faint microwave glow was discovered in 1964 coming from **every direction** in the sky. Its existence is very hard to explain any other way.

### A theory is not a fact
The Big Bang is currently the **only theory that explains all the observations**, which is why scientists accept it. But a scientific theory is always open to change if new evidence arrives.

A rival idea, the **Steady State theory**, proposed that the Universe had always looked the same, with new matter created to fill the gaps as it expanded. It could explain red-shift but **not** the cosmic microwave background, so it was abandoned.

The Big Bang theory does not explain what came *before* the expansion or *why* it started. Those remain open questions.

question.text: Which TWO pieces of evidence support the Big Bang theory?
question.hint: One concerns galaxies, the other a faint glow across the whole sky.
question.explanation: The red-shift of distant galaxies (showing expansion) and the cosmic microwave background radiation both support the Big Bang. Seasons are due to Earth's tilt, and moon phases to its orbit; neither says anything about the Universe's origin.

options.text: The red-shift of light from distant galaxies

activities.title: An accelerating Universe and the unknowns
activities.content:
## A surprise from supernovae

A particular type of supernova always explodes with about the same brightness, so it can be used as a 'standard candle': how dim it looks tells you how far away it is. Since 1998 astronomers have used very **distant supernovae** to measure how the expansion has changed over time.

Everyone expected gravity to be **slowing** the expansion down. Instead the measurements showed that distant galaxies are receding **faster than expected**: the expansion of the Universe is **speeding up**.

## Dark energy
Something must be pushing space apart against gravity. Scientists call it **dark energy**, but nobody knows what it is. It appears to make up about 70 % of the energy content of the Universe.

## Dark matter
There is a second mystery. Galaxies **rotate faster** than the gravity of their visible stars and gas could allow; they should fly apart. The extra gravity must come from matter that **does not emit or absorb light** and so cannot be seen directly: **dark matter**. Its effects are clear, but its nature is unknown. It seems to outweigh normal matter about five to one.

## Why this matters
These discoveries show that our understanding of the Universe is **incomplete**. Only about 5 % of the Universe is the ordinary matter we understand. Scientists are still collecting evidence, and the model may change again, which is exactly how science is supposed to work.

question.text: Match each idea to the observation that led to it.
question.hint: Dark energy is about expansion; dark matter is about galaxies spinning.
question.explanation: Distant supernovae showed the expansion is accelerating, leading to the idea of dark energy. Galaxies rotating too fast for their visible mass led to dark matter. The cosmic microwave background is evidence for the Big Bang itself.

pairs.right: Distant supernovae show the expansion of the Universe is speeding up
Galaxies rotate faster than their visible matter can explain
Microwave radiation is detected coming from all directions in space

question.text: Explain how the red-shift of light from galaxies leads to the conclusion that the Universe began with a Big Bang.
question.hint: Start with what red-shift shows, then think about running time backwards.
question.explanation: Red-shift shows galaxies are moving away from us, with more distant ones moving faster, so the Universe is expanding. If it is expanding now, everything was closer together in the past. Tracing this back, the Universe must have started from a very small, dense and hot point: the Big Bang.

markScheme.criterion: Red-shift shows galaxies are moving away / the more distant, the faster
So the Universe is expanding
Going back in time everything was closer / started from a very small, dense, hot point

question.text:
An astronomer records the spectra of two galaxies, P and Q. The dark absorption lines in the spectrum of galaxy Q are shifted further towards the red end than those of galaxy P.

(a) Explain what causes the dark lines in the spectrum to be shifted towards the red end. (2 marks)

(b) State what the difference in red-shift tells the astronomer about the two galaxies. (2 marks)

(c) Explain why the Big Bang theory is currently accepted by most scientists, even though it cannot explain everything about the Universe. (1 mark)
question.hint: For (b), think about both the speed and the distance of each galaxy.
question.explanation: (a) The galaxies are moving away from us, so the light waves are stretched to a longer wavelength (lower frequency). (b) Galaxy Q is moving away faster than P and is therefore further away. (c) It is the only theory that explains all the current evidence, including red-shift and the cosmic microwave background radiation.

markScheme.criterion: The galaxies are moving away from the observer / Earth
So the wavelength of the light is increased / stretched (frequency decreased)
Galaxy Q is moving away faster than P
Galaxy Q is further away than P
It is the only theory that explains all the observations / evidence such as red-shift and CMBR

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Red-shift**: light from a source moving **away** is observed with a **longer wavelength** and **lower frequency**. Spectral lines shift towards the red end.
- Light from **almost all galaxies is red-shifted**, and the **further** the galaxy, the **bigger** the red-shift: distant galaxies recede faster.
- This shows the **Universe is expanding**, so it was once much smaller: evidence for the **Big Bang**, which says the Universe began 13.8 billion years ago from a very small, hot, dense point.
- The **cosmic microwave background radiation** is further evidence for the Big Bang and rules out the Steady State theory.
- Distant **supernovae** show the expansion is **accelerating**, blamed on **dark energy**. Galaxies spin too fast for their visible mass, pointing to **dark matter**. Neither is understood: our model of the Universe is incomplete.

practiceQuestions.text: When a light source moves away from an observer, what happens to the observed wavelength of its light?
practiceQuestions.hint: Red is at the long-wavelength end of the visible spectrum.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Moving away stretches the waves, so the observed wavelength increases (and the frequency decreases).

metadata.blanksText: The light from distant galaxies is red-shifted, and the further away a galaxy is, the ___ its red-shift, showing that it is moving away ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: Distance and recession speed increase together.
practiceQuestions.explanation: More distant galaxies have a larger red-shift and are moving away faster.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: red-shift means that distant galaxies look redder because they contain more red stars.
practiceQuestions.hint: Red-shift is a change in wavelength of the light, not a change in the stars themselves.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Red-shift is a shift of the whole spectrum, including its dark lines, to longer wavelengths because the galaxy is moving away. It does not mean the stars are redder.

practiceQuestions.text: A spectral line at 400 nm in the laboratory is observed at 412 nm in the light from a galaxy. Calculate the red-shift as a fraction of the original wavelength.

The red-shift of galaxy A is 0.02 and the red-shift of galaxy B is 0.10. Galaxy A is 300 million light years away. Assuming red-shift is proportional to distance, estimate the distance to galaxy B in millions of light years.
practiceQuestions.hint: B's red-shift is 5 times larger, so it is about 5 times further away.

practiceQuestions.text: Approximately how long ago did the Big Bang happen?
practiceQuestions.hint: It is a little over three times the age of the Earth (4.6 billion years).
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Universe is about 13.8 billion years old.

options.feedback: That is the age of the Earth and the solar system.

practiceQuestions.text: Put these statements in a logical order to build the argument for the Big Bang.
practiceQuestions.hint: Start with the observation and end with the conclusion.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Observation (red-shift) → interpretation (moving away, faster when further) → expanding Universe → was smaller in the past → began from a tiny hot dense point.
order: Light from distant galaxies is red-shifted
The galaxies are moving away, and more distant galaxies move faster
In the past the galaxies were much closer together
The Universe began from a very small, hot and dense point

practiceQuestions.text: Which TWO statements about dark matter and dark energy are correct?
practiceQuestions.hint: Both are inferred from their effects, not seen directly.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Dark energy is the name given to whatever is causing the accelerating expansion; dark matter is inferred from the rotation of galaxies. Neither can be seen directly and neither is well understood.

options.text: Dark energy is thought to be causing the expansion of the Universe to speed up
Dark matter is inferred from the way galaxies rotate
Dark matter can be seen with powerful telescopes
options.feedback: Dark matter does not emit or absorb light; it is invisible.

options.text: Scientists fully understand what dark energy is made of

practiceQuestions.text: Observations of distant supernovae in 1998 surprised astronomers. Describe what they found and what it suggests.
practiceQuestions.hint: They expected gravity to slow the expansion.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The supernovae were dimmer, so further away, than expected: distant galaxies are receding faster than predicted, meaning the expansion of the Universe is accelerating rather than slowing. This suggests something, called dark energy, is pushing the expansion.

markScheme.criterion: The expansion of the Universe is speeding up / galaxies receding faster than expected
Suggests the existence of dark energy / something opposing gravity

practiceQuestions.text:
The Steady State theory once competed with the Big Bang theory. Both could explain the red-shift of galaxies.

(a) Describe the observation, made in 1964, that led most scientists to reject the Steady State theory. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why scientists still say the Big Bang theory might have to be changed in the future. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (a), think about radiation arriving from all directions. For (b), think about what the theory cannot yet explain.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Microwave radiation (the cosmic microwave background) was detected coming from every direction in space; the Big Bang predicts it as the stretched remains of the early Universe's radiation, but the Steady State theory cannot explain it. (b) Scientific theories are always provisional. There are observations the theory does not yet explain, such as the accelerating expansion (dark energy) and the extra gravity in galaxies (dark matter), so new evidence could change or replace it.

markScheme.criterion: Cosmic microwave background radiation was detected
Coming from all directions / predicted by Big Bang but not by Steady State
There are things the theory does not explain, e.g. dark energy / dark matter / accelerating expansion
New evidence / observations could change the theory; theories are provisional

practiceQuestions.text: The dark lines in the spectrum of a galaxy appear at longer wavelengths than the same lines measured from a lamp in the laboratory. What does this show about the galaxy?
practiceQuestions.hint: A longer wavelength than expected is a red-shift. Which direction of motion stretches the waves?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The lines have been shifted towards the red end of the spectrum, which means the light waves have been stretched to a longer wavelength. This happens when the source is moving away from the observer.

options.text: The galaxy is moving away from us
The galaxy is moving towards us
options.feedback: Movement towards us would squash the waves, giving a blue-shift.

options.text: The galaxy is hotter than the Sun
options.feedback: The shift of the lines is about motion, not temperature.

options.text: The galaxy contains more hydrogen than ours

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: the galaxies that are moving away from us the fastest are, in general, the most distant ones.
practiceQuestions.hint: How does the size of a galaxy's red-shift depend on its distance?
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Observations show that the further away a galaxy is, the larger its red-shift, and a larger red-shift means a faster speed of recession. So the most distant galaxies are moving away fastest.

practiceQuestions.text: A hydrogen line has a wavelength of 600 nm when measured in the laboratory. In the light from a galaxy the same line is observed at 618 nm. Calculate the red-shift as a fraction of the original wavelength. Give your answer as a decimal.
practiceQuestions.hint: Find the increase in wavelength first, then divide it by the laboratory wavelength.

practiceQuestions.text: Which TWO observations are explained by the Big Bang theory?
practiceQuestions.hint: One observation is about the light from galaxies; the other is a faint signal that fills the whole sky.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The light from distant galaxies is red-shifted, showing that the Universe is expanding from a starting point, and the cosmic microwave background radiation is the leftover radiation from the hot early Universe. Comets returning on schedule and craters on the Moon are explained by gravity and impacts, not by the origin of the Universe.

options.text: Light from distant galaxies is shifted to longer wavelengths
A faint background of microwave radiation is detected from every direction in space
Comets return to the inner solar system at regular intervals
options.feedback: This is explained by gravity and orbits, not by the Big Bang.

options.text: The Moon is covered in craters
options.feedback: Craters are caused by impacts, not by the origin of the Universe.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each scientific idea to the observation that led to it.
practiceQuestions.hint: Expansion comes from red-shift; dark matter is about how galaxies spin; dark energy is about how the expansion is changing.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The red-shift of galaxies increasing with distance showed that the Universe is expanding. Stars near the edges of galaxies orbit faster than the visible matter can account for, which led to the idea of dark matter. Measurements of very distant supernovae showed the expansion is speeding up, which led to the idea of dark energy.

pairs.right: The red-shift of galaxies increases with their distance from us
Stars at the edges of galaxies orbit faster than the visible mass can explain
Measurements of very distant supernovae show the expansion is speeding up

practiceQuestions.text: The light from galaxy Z shows a much larger red-shift than the light from galaxy Y. Explain what this tells us about the two galaxies and how such observations support the Big Bang theory.
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the speeds and distances of the two galaxies first, then think about what a Universe that is spreading out must have looked like long ago.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The larger red-shift means galaxy Z is moving away from us faster than Y, and because red-shift increases with distance, Z is also further away. Galaxies everywhere are moving apart in this way, so the Universe is expanding. If it is expanding now, everything must have been closer together in the past, so the Universe began from a very small, dense and hot point: the Big Bang.

markScheme.criterion: Galaxy Z is moving away faster / is further away than Y
This shows the Universe is expanding
Going back in time everything was closer together / began from a very small, dense, hot point

practiceQuestions.text:
A telescope records the spectra of two galaxies, M and N. The absorption lines in the spectrum of galaxy M are shifted further towards the red end than those of galaxy N.

(a) Explain why the absorption lines from a galaxy are shifted towards the red end of the spectrum. (2 marks)

(b) State what the difference between the two red-shifts tells the astronomer about galaxies M and N. (2 marks)

(c) Scientists' model of the Universe has changed many times. Explain why it may change again in the future. (1 mark)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (a), think about what happens to the wavelength of waves from a source that is moving away. For (b), consider both speed and distance.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) The galaxies are moving away from the Earth, so the light waves are stretched to a longer wavelength and a lower frequency. (b) Galaxy M is moving away faster than galaxy N, and is therefore further away. (c) New evidence from better telescopes and instruments may not fit the current model, so the model would have to be changed or replaced.

markScheme.criterion: The galaxies are moving away from the observer / Earth
So the wavelength of the light is increased / stretched (frequency decreased)
Galaxy M is moving away faster than N
Galaxy M is further away than N
New evidence / observations from better instruments may not fit the current model
